Can I stay with this moment without making it worse?
We do not go looking for the island. We become it.

The bee takes the nourishment it needs and leaves no wound behind.
Can I give myself wholeheartedly to something without making winning the condition for my peace?
Balance is not standing still. It is the quiet inner strength that allows us to respond wisely.
To practise metta is to remember that beneath our defences, there is still a friendly heart waiting to be uncovered.
Our words aren't only meant to be spoken — they're meant to be lived.
Each return is an opportunity to practise patience and attention.
Effort can reach a point where it gets in the way.
Non-hate sits closer with equanimity — a refusal to swing to extremes, and a choice of not picking at our own wounds.
When we loosen our grip on perceived certainty, there is room for curiosity.
Awakening, healing, and growth rarely happen through one dramatic breakthrough. More often than not, they are the fruit of choosing to show up, one breath, one step, one day at a time.

posts.title: The Quiet Work of Change
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 99: How properly tending to conditions will allow results to develop
posts.body_text:
It is easy to want a calmer mind and then become impatient with the effort involved. 

We sit down to meditate, encounter the familiar distraction or drowsiness, and wonder whether anything is really changing. The wish for progress can itself become a hindrance. 

In the Nava Sutta, the Buddha describes a hen caring for her eggs. Wishing for them to hatch is insufficient; she must provide warmth and proper incubation. The teaching invites us to consider the conditions we create for our own development. If we want to grow, we have to create the conditions that support our growth.

Our practice can draw on four qualities associated with the four bases of power: aspiration, energy, intent, and investigation. Applied to everyday practice, these offer practical guidance:

(1) Remember why we practise. 
(2) Make the effort sustainable. 
(3) Give it our attention and will. 
(4) Examine what helps or doesn’t, and adjust accordingly.

This might mean putting the phone aside, asking for twenty uninterrupted minutes, or choosing a time when we are more alert. If evening meditation repeatedly ends in drowsiness, trying the morning is a useful experiment. If we miss a day, begin again. Curiosity makes it easier to learn from these experiences without turning them into judgments about ourselves.

The same sutta describes a carpenter whose tool handle gradually wears down through daily use. The incremental change is difficult to measure, yet its cumulative effect becomes apparent. This offers a helpful perspective when we feel compelled to assess every meditation session.

During a meditation like the body scan, this work is quiet and straightforward: notice sensations, recognise when attention has wandered, and return. Each return is an opportunity to practise patience and attention. Each practice creates the conditions for the transformation we want to see. 

---

Over 10 and 11 October, the Take A Pause community reflected on “the quiet work of change” and patiently practiced the body scan together. We closed the session with the reading of the poem “The Seedling” by Paul Laurence Dunbar.

posts.title: My Wellbeing, Our Wellbeing
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 98: How tending to ourselves transforms the way we meet one another
posts.body_text:
Wellbeing may feel personal, yet it shapes our shared lives. This was the key theme of the latest Take A Pause Live session.

We turned to the Sedaka Sutta (SN 47.19), which describes a metaphor of two acrobats balancing on a bamboo pole. Each acrobat must attend to their own balance for both of them to be safe. 

The teaching goes further: cultivating mindfulness protects both ourselves and others. 

When we tend to our own mind and body, we are at the same time taking care of our relationship with others. 

And when we choose to meet others with patience, harmlessness, goodwill, and sympathy, these qualities, in turn, help steady us.

Imagine a tense morning at home or a difficult conversation at work. When we pause to notice a tight jaw, tiredness, or a flash of impatience, we gain a moment to choose our response more wisely. This pause is what keeps a hurtful remark or unwholesome behaviour from landing on someone else. 

And when we listen with attentiveness and compassion to a person who is struggling, the sense of balance, steadiness and ease we are cultivating within will protect us.

In our meditation, we were invited to begin with the body: watch what is present, notice any worry or fatigue, and resist the urge to judge or fix it. 

We were reminded that no perfect calm was required, and that honest awareness and acceptance of each moment offered a useful place to start.

From there, we considered how an inner state might shape the next interaction with our experience. 

We reflected on the nature of cause and effect — how a reaction to an inner state can translate into impulses and behaviours that impact our outer landscape. 

Erin also introduced mettā, the practice of offering kind wishes to ourselves and others. 

We might quietly wish for patience with our feelings and enough space to respond wisely. Then we can extend that wish to the people sharing our day.

A key takeaway from practising together: Our wellbeing is interconnected. Caring for ourselves gives us more room to care for others, and caring for others can strengthen the qualities that sustain our own peace of mind.

---

posts.title: A View is Not The Whole
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 97: Making room for what we don’t yet know
posts.body_text:
How often do we feel certain about someone or something, only to realise later that we did not have the whole picture?

In a recent Take A Pause live session, we reflected on an old Buddhist story of people — blind by birth — who were each shown only one part of an elephant. 

One felt its ear and described it as a basket. Another touched its foot and insisted it was like a post. 

Each had encountered something real. Yet each mistook that one part for the whole animal, and soon they were arguing over who was right.

We can easily recognise this in our own lives. 

Someone raises their voice… that is what happened. We feel afraid… that is what we felt. 

Then, very quickly, the mind adds a judgement: “They wanted to hurt me.” 

Perhaps they did. Perhaps something else was happening. We do not yet know.

This is where a pause can help. 

We can ask: What do I know for sure? What am I feeling? What meaning have I given this moment? 

These questions are not about dismissing our thoughts and feelings. They help us notice the difference between our experience and our interpretation of it.

We can practise this in meditation, too. 

Listen to the sounds around you. Feel the body, notice the breath. When a thought arises about a sound, notice the thought and any impulse to follow it. Then gently return to what is actually here.

A view can be very useful, and it may even hold some truth. 

But when we loosen our grip on perceived certainty, there is room for curiosity, and for what we have not yet seen.

---

posts.title: When Persistence Stops Working
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 96: Knowing when to adjust our efforts
posts.body_text:
We are often encouraged to keep going. Persistence is celebrated as a sign of strength, and when something isn’t working, we tend to assume we just need to try harder.

But effort can reach a point where it gets in the way.

In the Sona Sutta, a monk practises walking meditation until his feet bleed. Despite his dedication, he feels he is making no progress and considers giving up.

The Buddha asks him about the lute he used to play, and helps him understand that strings that are too tight or too loose cannot make music properly. They need the right tension.

Our effort needs this kind of adjustment too.

We can recognise it in meditation. 

We want to be calmer, get frustrated when the mind wanders, and begin criticising ourselves. Practice becomes another thing we expect ourselves to perform well at.

At Take A Pause Live, we explored three qualities of attention: straining, drifting, and relaxed alertness.

Relaxed alertness allows us to stay engaged with patience and interest. When we notice strain in the mind and body, we soften our effort. When we are drifting, we gently bring our attention back to the present moment.

This same awareness can support everyday life. 

We might prepare thoughtfully for a conversation while loosening our attachment to how it turns out, or take a pause during work when we know another hour of pushing is getting us nowhere.

We can learn to recognise our need for rest without feeling guilty about it.

Each new moment offers a chance to adjust and recalibrate.

With skill and wisdom, this is what we learn to ask ourselves: 

How much effort does this moment — right here, right now — actually need?

---

posts.title: What Truly Matters
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 95: What deserves your limited number of days?
posts.body_text:
As we closed our Dhammapada-inspired series on Insight Timer last weekend, the final theme of “what truly matters” reminded us of the importance of practice.

Verses 11 and 12, in Gil Fronsdal’s translation, say that those who mistake the inessential to be essential, and the essential as inessential, never reach the essential. 

Inessential here does not mean bad or wrong. Rather, it points out what is not necessary or not important.

We are often too close to our own lives to see this. 

So imagine someone else looking at how you spend your time, your energy and your attention. 

What would they conclude that you believe matters most?

There is usually a gap between what we say matters to us and what our life reveals to matter to us. 

We say family is everything, and then we sit with them without being present. We say we want a simple life, and then we fill every moment with stimulation. We say meditation is a priority, and then we postpone it for everything else.

So part of the practice is telling the urgent apart from the important. 

Modern life makes everything feel urgent, with the notifications, the updates, and the deadlines. 

What is truly essential tends to come quietly. It is the conversation we keep avoiding, the body that has been struggling in the background. 

It helps to ask: 

Does this need my attention because it demands it, or because it truly matters to me?

The final verses turn to reflections on mortality, which is heavy — and meant to be. They are not there to create despair, but drive a healthy sense of urgency. 

Time is finite, and a mindful life does not just drop into our lap. We have to cultivate it, and that takes effort and practice.

This was the closing reflection I left the community with: 

What deserves your limited number of days?

---

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 12-13 September 2026, we reflected on where we would like to expend our time, attention, and energy. We then listened to the poem When Death Comes by Mary Oliver.

posts.title: The Path Beneath Our Feet
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 94: Only when walking happens can the benefits of walking happen.
posts.body_text:
Seven sessions into our Dhammapada series, we arrive at the chapter called The Path. The path here is the Noble Eightfold Path - right view, right intention, right speech, and the rest.

This is the path I have proclaimed, Having pulled out the arrows. It is up to you to make strong effort. Tathagatas merely tell you how. 

(verse 276, trans. Gil Fronsdal)

Tathagatas are those who have arrived at the truth. They tell you about the ‘how’, and that is all they can do. 

You may revere your teacher and trust the teachings completely, and still the walking is yours and yours alone. Your teacher cannot walk the path for you.

Understanding the path is not the same as standing on it. We can name everything that’s required for walking the path and still not have put our feet down. 

Only when walking happens can the benefits of walking happen.

Wisdom arises from practice. Without practice, it decays.

(verse 282, trans. Gil Fronsdal)

Cause and effect, stated plainly. Practice, and wisdom grows. Leave it, and knowledge stays knowledge, never becoming a true knowing.

The Buddha did not ask for these words to be believed. Ehipassiko, he said - come and see for yourself. So there is nothing here to take on faith. 

A path becomes a path only when it is walked.

And there is no need to wait, for the path is right under our feet. 

It is in everyday life — how we hold our minds this morning, in what our hands do today, in the words we offer the people in front of us. 

It is also remarkably simple — do no harm, engage in what is skilful, and purify your own mind. 

May we all start walking, and keep walking. 

---

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 5-6 September 2026, we practiced walking the path right here, right now, through mindfulness meditation. We then shared a reading from Erin Lee’s Take A Pause: Waking Up to a Life of Clarity.

posts.title: The Scent of a Life Well Lived
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 93: May we move through this world gently
posts.body_text:
Six sessions into our Dhammapada-inspired series, we arrive at the chapter called Flowers.

As a bee gathers nectar 
And moves on without harming 
The flower, its color, or its fragrance, 
Just so should a sage walk through a village.

(verse 49, trans. Gil Fronsdal)

The bee takes the nourishment it needs and leaves no wound behind. 

Now don’t be mistaken — this is not a call to have no impact at all. It is an invitation to thoughtful participation. Instead of asking what we can get from a place, we can be more cognisant of what we will leave behind once we have passed through it. 

Can I disagree with someone without humiliating them? Can I receive care from a community without taking it for granted?

Verse 50 then turns our attention inward.

It is easy to look outward and begin sorting the world into what should and shouldn’t be done. This verse asks us to turn the other way first and ask what I have done, and what I have left undone. 

Cultivating goodness is self-cultivation before it is anything else, and looking inward is what keeps it from hardening into self-righteousness.

Just as from a heap of flowers 
Many garlands can be made, 
So you, with your mortal life, 
Should do many skillful things.

(verse 53, trans. Gil Fronsdal)

Goodness is rarely one heroic act. Instead, it is often found in many ordinary moments: the tray returned at the food court, the trolley pushed back at the supermarket, the cruel post we decline to forward on our socials. 

A life is fragrant because of the little good things we repeatedly do.

Verses 54 to 56 tell us that the scent of a virtuous person travels even against the wind. 

So think of who has quietly influenced you on one way or another — an acquaintance who treats service staff with respect, a colleague who never joins the office gossip. 

Flowers are not fragrant because we are watching them. Likewise, goodness is not meant to be performative; it quietly influences through embodiment. 

Verses 58 and 59 leave us with the image of a sweet-smelling lotus growing in a heap of rubbish. 

We have a saying — “no mud, no lotus.” The messiness of our lives is not what we have to clear away before practice begins. It is what we practice with, and through this mess, wisdom and compassion emerge, and the scent of goodness arrives. 

May we move through the world gently, and thoughtfully. 

---

posts.title: The Happiness Chapter
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Episode 92: A practice of putting down, rather than adding.
posts.body_text:
Five sessions into our Dhammapada series, we arrive at the theme of happiness. The teachings are so often heard as suffering, suffering, suffering… and yet there really is a whole chapter on happiness.

Ah, so happily we live, without ambition among those with ambition.

(verse 199, trans. Gil Fronsdal)

Now don’t be mistaken — this is not about withdrawing from the world. We are part of this ecosystem, and we are participating. 

We simply stop letting its agitations reproduce inside us. 

Someone else’s anger in the office does not have to become our anger. 

A consumer culture repeating “more, more, more” does not have to turn into a sense of lacking within us.

The text tells us that victory gives birth to hate, that the defeated sleep in anguish, and that those who give up both sleep happily. 

Modern life is very much organised around a scoreboard — who performed better, whose opinion won, who was right. 

There is suffering on both sides of that board, and this includes the winning side, when we hold tightly to what we win.

There is nothing wrong with winning, of course, and nothing wrong with aspiration; in fact, our practice carries one of the largest aspirations of all — the complete freedom from suffering. 

The invitation is a little quieter: 

Can I give myself wholeheartedly to something without making winning the condition for my peace?

With this, our understanding of happiness moves from a merely pleasurable experience to freedom from what we are bound to or compelled by.

Happiness comes from what we choose to put down, not what we acquire or add to our lives.

So this week, before reaching for one more thing, let us notice what is already present, and see that just being here, alive and breathing, is perhaps enough.

---

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 22-23 August 2026, we cultivated a sense of enough-ness with a body awareness meditation. We then listened to the poem, So Much Happiness, by Naomi Shihab Nye.

posts.title: An Island Within
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 91: Staying steady with our inner refuge
posts.body_text:
Four sessions into our Dhammapada-inspired series, the text offers us a few metaphors:

Through effort, vigilance, 
Restraint, and self-control, 
The wise person can become an island 
No flood will overwhelm.

(verse 25, trans. Gil Fronsdal)

We do not go looking for the island. We become it.

The floods in our life are ordinary enough. They are other people’s opinions of your work, a conflict you did not ask for, the plain uncertainty of being alive. 

They come and go as they wish, and they will not stop coming because you have started practicing.

The text then turns from water to wind: 

A solid mass of rock is not moved by the wind (verse 81).

In the teachings there are eight worldly winds - gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disrepute. The pleasant four blow just as hard as the others, only because we hold them tightly and they leave anyway.

Now don’t be mistaken — being a rock is not being cold, or unresponsive, or hidden away. The rock sits bravely out in the open. It meets the wind, and it stays.

Oneself, indeed, is one’s own protector. What other protector could there be? (verse 160)

This verse sits in a chapter called Oneself, which is not about self-importance. It is about ownership. 

We can have teachers we trust and wise friends we lean on, but they guide us from outside. 

Taking ownership of our own mind means staying with ourselves in difficulty rather than abandoning ourselves there, and being willing to say: I am worth this effort.

---

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 15-16 August 2026, we cultivated our inner refuge through staying with the body in the midst of “floods” and “winds”. We shared a reading from Erin’s book, Take A Pause: Waking Up to a Life of Clarity.

posts.title: Better Than A Thousand Words
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 90: On saying less, and living what we say
posts.body_text:
We live in an age of too many words. 

Content is constantly produced, and constantly consumed. We’re communicating more, but are we communicating better?

The Dhammapada puts it plainly: 

“Better than a thousand meaningless statements is one meaningful word which, having been heard, brings peace” (verses 100-102, trans. Gil Fronsdal). 

Not more words, but wiser ones.

Then this, from the same text: 

“Like a beautiful flower, brightly coloured but lacking scent, so are well-spoken words, fruitless when not carried out” (verses 51-52, trans. Gil Fronsdal). 

A flower can look lovely and still have nothing to give. So can our words.

Carried out — that’s the phrase I keep returning to. 

Our words aren’t only meant to be spoken - they’re meant to be lived. So the question isn’t did I say the right thing, but is there a gap between what I say and how I actually live? Is there alignment between my speech and my action, or is there dissonance?

I always sit with this one. I can speak very beautifully about compassion, and then find myself snapping at my family. I can give someone gentle advice about patience, and then lose my temper at a service counter minutes later. The words were true. They just weren’t carried out.

This is where restraint comes in, and I want to clarify a possible misreading of it. Restraint is not suppression. It’s self-regulation - noticing the anger, the judgement, the opinion forming, and knowing it doesn’t have to become that sarcastic email, the harmful gossip, the harsh comment.

Mindful speech isn’t about being agreeable, either. It can be firm, with boundaries. It just has to be skillful and wise.

So before your next difficult conversation, ask yourself: what impact will my words have? What do I want my words to leave behind?

---

posts.title: The Freedom Beyond Anger
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 89: Peace of mind that is not dependent on anyone else
posts.body_text:
Think about something that irritated you recently — perhaps not a deep wound, just a tone in a message or a decision made without you. 

Notice how readily the mind returns to it, and starts obsessing over it, even now.

The Dhammapada is interested in exactly that kind of fixation. 

The text from this ancient collection of teachings doesn’t deny that something happened to us. It points at what the mind does afterwards — in the endless replaying and rehearsing. 

When a story is repeated enough, it can stop feeling like a memory and start to feel like a fact about who we are. This identification is where suffering sets in, rather than in the event itself. 

“Hatred never ends through hatred. By non-hate alone does it end,” says the teachings. 

Non-hate here doesn’t equate to love. The practice doesn’t ask you to feel affection towards someone who hurt you, nor is forgiveness the entry fee. 

Non-hate sits closer with equanimity — a refusal to swing to extremes, and a choice of not picking at our own wounds. 

The Dhammapada draws a useful distinction between someone who works skilfully with anger — called a charioteer, and everyone else — merely a rein-holder: composed on the outside but still seething underneath. 

Suppression can easily be mistaken as having control over the emotion.

The freedom beyond anger being described here isn’t tolerance, and it isn’t passivity in the face of harm either. 

It’s the capacity to meet a person or situation we don’t like with greater ease. 

It is the ability to enjoy peace of mind without being dependent on someone else changing.

---

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 1-2 August 2026, we practiced watching anger show up in the body and mind, moment by moment, with awareness and equanimity. We closed the session with a reading from Erin Lee’s Take A Pause: Waking up to a life of clarity.

posts.title: The Mind Leads the Way
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 88: How thoughts shape our experiences
posts.body_text:
Two people can walk away from the same experience with completely different stories. 

One replays it all evening, simmering. The other has already moved on. Same event, different state of mind.

The Dhammapada opens with this: 

Every experience is shaped by the mind that meets it. An agitated mind, and stress trails you like a shadow; a settled mind, and ease follows just as faithfully (v. 1-2). 

This is, most straightforwardly, cause and effect.

The mind is a natural storyteller — constantly predicting, replaying, catastrophising, judging, comparing, often before we’ve finished our coffee. 

The Dhammapada calls the mind “hard to control, flighty, alighting where it wishes”, but emphasises that it can be tamed, and that a watched mind brings happiness (v. 33–36). 

The goal isn’t to silence the inner chatter, but to notice it: catch a spiralling thought, see it as just a thought — a mental event — rather than a verdict on reality, and let it pass instead of grasping at it.

This doesn’t mean that all hardship or misfortune is the mind’s fault, or that positive thinking fixes our problems — plenty of conditions sit outside our control. But one verse from the text puts it plainly: 

A poorly directed mind does more harm than an enemy, while a well-directed one does more good than your own parents (v. 42–43). 

The conversation inside our own head is the one thing we always get to work with, not because nothing else matters, but because it’s the one lever we get to hold.

This, fundamentally, is a practice of ownership — learning to meet our thoughts differently, rather than being run by them. 

However each moment unfolds, the mind leads the way.

Note: Verse translations are from The Dhammapada, trans. Gil Fronsdal (Shambhala, 2006).

---

posts.title: The Capacity to Remain Balanced
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 87: Staying grounded no matter how the winds blow
posts.body_text:
We often imagine balance as a life in which nothing difficult happens. 

But a life with upekkha, translated as equanimity, is not absent of disruption. It is having the capacity to remain steady and grounded while everything continues to move. 

The Pali word upekkha suggests “looking on steadily” — meeting each experience with clarity rather than indifference. 

Praise and blame, gain and loss, recognition and criticism, pleasure and pain: these winds are always blowing. 

Equanimity does not ask us to avoid them, suppress our feelings, or become emotionally distant. 

It helps us notice when we are being pulled too strongly towards what we like, or pushed away by what we dislike.

This steadiness matters especially when we care deeply. Without it, generosity can become depletion, determination can become strain, and compassion can become burnout. 

With equanimity, we can offer care without being overly fixated on outcomes we cannot control.

The practice begins in ordinary moments: noticing pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral experiences without immediately grasping, resisting, or drifting away. 

In other words, we learn to stay present without being swept away.

Balance is not standing still. 

It is the quiet inner strength that allows us to respond wisely, offer care sustainably, and hold the results of our efforts a little more lightly each day.

---

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 18-19 July 2026, we practiced cultivating equanimity towards pleasant and unpleasant experiences. We closed the session with a reading of the poem Me Imperturbe by Walt Whitman.

posts.title: Uncovering a Friendly Heart
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 86: What unconditional goodwill means
posts.body_text:
Metta is often translated as loving-kindness, and at its root is something very simple: friendliness. 

Not so much politeness, not people-pleasing, and definitely not pretending everything is fine. 

A friendly heart is one that learns to wish well, even when life feels difficult, even when another person is difficult, even when we ourselves feel difficult to love.

This does not mean we abandon boundaries. 

We can say no, disagree, walk away, or hold someone accountable, and still choose not to feed hatred and hostility in our own hearts. 

Metta is not weakness. 

It is a quiet strength that helps us soften the sharp edges of resentment without denying what has happened.

The practice can begin simply. 

Bring to mind someone you care for and offer a few quiet phrases: May you be happy. May you be healthy. 

Then, slowly, extend the same wishes to yourself, to someone neutral, to someone challenging, and eventually to all beings.

Some days, the words may feel mechanical, and that is okay. 

The heart does not always open dramatically. Sometimes it softens subtly, almost imperceptibly.

To practise metta is to remember that beneath our defences, there is still a friendly heart waiting to be uncovered.

At Take A Pause Live on Insight Timer over 11 - 12 July 2026, we practiced extending thoughts of kindness and unconditional goodwill to ourselves and others. We closed the session with a reading from the book Loving Kindness in Plain English by Bhante Gunaratana.

posts.title: Committing Wholeheartedly
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 85: Holding steady when things get hard
posts.body_text:
There is a quality of heart the teachings call adhiṭṭhāna — determination, resolve, the kind of commitment that holds steady when things get hard. 

It isn’t sheer willpower, and it isn’t rigidity. Adhiṭṭhāna is something more grounded than that.

At my first Vipassana retreat, I learned what it really means to stay. 

The instruction was simple: do your best not to move. No shifting posture, no opening your eyes. 

I took it seriously, and what followed was some of the most intense discomfort I’d ever sat with. Physical pain, mental anguish, swirling anxiety, burning anger, the urge to get up and walk out. 

But I stayed. 

And at some point, something changed. The pain was still there, but it no longer had the same hold on me. I felt calm, even aware. 

That was my first real taste and cultivation of adhiṭṭhāna.

In everyday life, we tend toward extremes — pushing hard, then giving up entirely when results don’t come quickly. 

Adhiṭṭhāna is what keeps us from falling back into that cycle. More than motivation, which comes and goes, this is a deeper commitment to staying the course.

And when we lapse? We begin again. That, too, is part of the practice.

---

posts.title: Being Real and Honest
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 84: A practice of living in alignment with reality
posts.body_text:
What does it mean to truly be honest? Not just with others, but with ourselves?

In Buddhist teachings, there’s a quality of heart called sacca — often translated as truthfulness or authenticity. 

And it’s more than just not lying. 

It’s about living in alignment with reality: making sure our words, actions, and intentions actually match up.

In everyday life, this may be harder than it sounds.

We live in an age of curated identities. Social media nudges us into performance mode — presenting the best version of ourselves rather than the real one. 

Sacca invites us to pause and ask: Am I who I appear to be?

It also shows up in subtler ways. 

When we do something kind, is there a small ego boost in it? When we set a boundary, is fear quietly driving that decision? When we love someone, is it truly unconditional — or does it come with strings?

None of this is about self-judgment. It’s simply about seeing clearly.

And there’s a practical piece too: keeping our word. 

When we make a commitment, do you follow through?

Cultivating this kind of honesty — gently, without self-criticism — is one of the most grounding things we can do for ourselves and for everyone around us.

---

At Take A Pause Live over 20 & 21 June 2026, we practiced body awareness and learned to meet each moment of our experience truthfully, as it it. We closed the session with a reading of the poem Telescope by Louise Glück.

posts.title: The Strength to Stay
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 83: Patience as a quiet power
posts.body_text:
We often think of patience as something we simply have — or don’t have.

To us, it’s a personality trait, a virtue some people are born with, or something we tell ourselves to just be when things get difficult.

But khanti — patience as a quality of heart — is something far deeper than that.

It is the capacity to stay.

To stay when things don’t go your way.

To stay without collapsing, without retaliating, and without running away.

There is a teaching in the Buddhist tradition — a simile — that makes this viscerally clear. 

The Buddha described a scenario in which bandits cut a person apart with a saw, bone by bone. Even then, he said, a good practitioner does not let hatred take over the heart. 

It’s intentionally extreme, and we’re not meant to take it literally. That’s the nature of a simile — it stretches the imagination so the principle lands more deeply.

The point is this: no matter what comes at you, the heart can be protected.

Think about our modern-day saws. The meeting that runs over, the WiFi dropping right when we need it most. The message we’ve tried to communicate ten different ways, and still no one seems to understand. The illness that isn’t healing as quickly as we would like.

What are the saws in your life?

These moments of friction — small and large — are not obstacles to patience. They are the practice itself.

This is also a reframing of what it means to be strong.

We tend to associate strength with control: pushing through, winning, conquering. But khanti points us toward a different kind of strength — one that is deeply enduring.

It is the strength to remain present without being swept away.

Not suppressing what we feel, not tolerating harm, but meeting reality as it is, without immediately adding to our suffering through reactivity.

Can I stay with this moment without making it worse?

This simple question is the whole practice.

Khanti asks something of us in three directions:

Patience with discomfort. Life is full of things beyond our control. When we can’t immediately fix or escape what’s uncomfortable, we have a choice: to resist and suffer more, or to stay and meet it with some steadiness.

Patience with others. This isn’t about putting up with people, or staying in situations that harm us. It’s about bringing more wisdom and compassion into how we respond — even when someone is difficult, even when we feel misunderstood. Kind speech is a form of patience. It takes real inner strength to soften the edges of our words when we’re frustrated.

Patience with ourselves. This is perhaps the hardest one. We can be relentlessly harsh with ourselves — for not doing enough, not progressing fast enough, not being who we think we should be by now. Khanti invites us to trust a little more in the unfolding of our own path and becoming.

---

At Take A Pause Live over 13 & 14 June 2026, we practiced the body scan as a way of cultivating patience.

I won’t pretend the body scan is everyone’s favourite.

I hear this often: “Please, not the body scan. It’s too slow, too long, too much.”

And yet, that resistance is exactly why it’s so valuable for cultivating patience.

The body scan asks us to be with the body as it is — not to feel a certain way, not to reach a special state, but simply to notice what’s actually here. 

Pleasant, unpleasant, neutral. Comfortable, uncomfortable. Whatever your reality is, that is what you’re meeting.

And when the mind wanders — which it will — there will be that familiar flicker of impatience. Why can’t I focus? Why am I so restless? Why is this so hard?

Those are the very moments khanti asks us to stay.

---

We read the poem Wait by Galway Kinnell, and ended with some loving-kindness — a few quiet phrases offered to ourselves:

May I meet this moment with patience. 

May I protect my heart from hatred and agitation. 

May I breathe with this discomfort, one moment at a time. 

May I remain steady when things don’t go my way.

---

posts.title: Steady, Sustainable Effort
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 82: A wiser relationship with our energy
posts.body_text:
It’s 2026. How often are we still celebrating exhaustion as a badge of honour, or mistaking constant busyness for true effort? 

We push, strive, overextend, and tell ourselves we are simply being committed. 

And the parami of viriya invites us into a wiser relationship with energy.

Viriya is often translated as energy or effort, but it carries the spirit of courage — the courage to keep showing up, especially when life feels difficult. 

This doesn’t mean we force ourselves into exhaustion. And we certainly don’t have to swing to the other extreme of giving up, checking out, or “lying flat” — 躺平 (tǎng píng), as the trending Chinese phrase goes. 

We want to find the middle way between overexertion and passivity. 

Like tuning a string instrument, the effort cannot be too tight or too loose. It needs the right tension for harmony and balance to arise.

Investigating their relationship with viriya, the practitioner asks:

What is worth giving my energy to? What drains me unnecessarily? What supports clarity and well-being?

This is especially important in meditation. 

We show up for practice because it is well worth the effort. 

Each time the mind wanders, we begin again. Not harshly, not lazily, but steadily. 

Over time, this sustained effort becomes a quiet strength.

Awakening, healing, and growth rarely happen through one dramatic breakthrough. 

More often than not, they are the fruit of choosing to show up, one breath, one step, one day at a time. 

---

posts.title: Seeing Things Clearly
posts.subtitle: Take A Pause Ep. 81: Wisdom is not the same as intelligence.
posts.body_text:
When we think about wisdom, we may associate it with knowledge, intelligence, or years of experience. 

From the perspective of mindfulness, wisdom — or paññā — is something much more profound.

Wisdom is the ability to see things clearly.

It is the capacity to understand what leads to suffering and what leads away from it. 

It is recognising how fear, attachment, craving, and resistance shape our experience, and how often we create additional (and often unnecessary) struggle by holding on too tightly to what we want life to be.

In today’s world, we are surrounded by more information than ever before. We have access to endless opinions, perspectives, and advice. Yet despite all this knowledge, many of us still feel overwhelmed, reactive, and dissatisfied. Information alone does not guarantee wisdom.

Wisdom begins with pausing.

When we slow down and pay attention, we start to observe our thoughts, emotions, and habits more clearly. 

We notice what is helpful and what is not. We learn that not every thought deserves to be believed, and not every emotion needs to dictate our response.

Over time, wisdom reveals itself in ordinary moments: pausing before reacting in anger, letting go of the need to be right, or accepting that change is simply part of life.

Wisdom is not about becoming someone who is special or highly-regarded. 

It is learning to meet life as it is, with greater clarity, understanding, and ease.

---
